# Caliptra Top-Level Module Behavioral Specification

## 1. Overview

This module is the top-level integration point for the Caliptra security subsystem. It provides a complete, self-contained root-of-trust microcontroller subsystem, including a RISC-V processor, cryptographic engines, key and measurement storage, SoC communication, debug access, and configurable peripheral interfaces.

The module shall:

- Provide a secure, reset-controlled boot sequence that communicates readiness to the SoC.
- Expose a SoC-facing APB register interface for mailbox communication, fuse loading, security control, and status reporting.
- Integrate an internal RISC-V processor with local instruction and data memory.
- Provide cryptographic services to firmware, including hashing, HMAC, ECC, key vault, PCR vault, data vault, and de-obfuscation.
- Handle security state, debug mode, scan mode, and secret clearing.
- Generate interrupts and error indications to the SoC and to the internal processor.
- Support optional internal TRNG, QSPI, and UART functionality based on build-time configuration.

## 2. Reset and Boot Behavior

### 2.1 Power and Reset Conditioning

The module shall sample a single power-good input and a single active-low reset input.

- Deassertion of power-good shall cause a power-on reset of the entire module.
- Reset deassertion after power-good shall initiate a warm-reset boot flow.
- All internal state shall be initialized to a known reset value whenever power-good is deasserted.

### 2.2 Boot Phases

The boot controller shall sequence the module through distinct readiness phases and expose these phases to the SoC through dedicated output indications.

The module shall:

1. Assert the fuse-ready output after reset is released, indicating that the SoC may program fuses.
2. Wait for the SoC to indicate that fuse programming is complete.
3. After fuse completion, advance to the firmware-loading phase and assert the firmware-push-ready output.
4. Once runtime firmware is ready, assert the runtime-ready output.

The readiness outputs shall be deasserted when their corresponding phase is not active.

The module shall also accept a boot breakpoint input. When this input is asserted, the boot controller shall stop advancing from the fuse phase and hold the module in its current boot state. The module shall resume only after the breakpoint is removed and the SoC writes the appropriate boot-FSM go command through the APB interface.

### 2.3 Fuse Programming

Fuse programming shall be accepted only during the fuse-ready boot phase. Once fuse programming is completed and locked:

- Further fuse writes shall be rejected.
- A read of a fuse location shall return the programmed fuse value.
- Fuse values shall persist across warm reset, but the fuse-completion indication must be written again by the SoC after each warm-reset boot sequence.

### 2.4 Firmware Update Reset

The module shall support a firmware-update reset flow that resets only the internal RISC-V processor while preserving the rest of the subsystem.

When triggered by an APB register write, the module shall:

- Hold the processor in reset for a programmable number of clock cycles.
- Keep all non-processor logic active and preserve memory contents.
- Force the internal bus to an idle state during the reset window.
- Unlock the instruction memory so new firmware can be loaded.
- Release the processor from reset after the programmed wait period.
- Resume normal operation with the existing firmware update flow.

## 3. Clock and Power Management

The module shall provide an internal clock-gating capability controlled by firmware.

When clock gating is enabled and the processor is halted, the module shall disable the gated clocks to:

- Cryptographic engines
- Vaults
- Mailbox SRAM
- Peripheral blocks
- Internal AHB fabric

The module shall keep the necessary always-on logic running so that reset, watchdog, and wake-up detection remain functional.

The module shall re-enable all gated clocks when any of the following conditions occur:

- The processor exits the halted state.
- A fatal error is asserted.
- The module enters debug mode or scan mode.
- A JTAG debug access is attempted.
- A change is detected on the generic input bus.
- An APB transaction is received from the SoC.

An APB transaction alone shall be sufficient to wake only the SoC interface clock domain. If no other wake condition is present and the processor remains halted, the other gated clocks may remain disabled after the APB transaction completes.

## 4. SoC APB Interface

The module shall provide an APB slave interface to the SoC. It shall respond to valid APB reads and writes according to the APB protocol.

### 4.1 General Access Rules

The APB interface shall:

- Perform 32-bit aligned accesses only.
- Return zero read data for accesses to undefined addresses.
- Drop writes to undefined addresses.
- Assert an APB error response for undefined or illegal accesses.
- Drop writes that do not have a valid requester attribute, if requester filtering is enabled.
- Assert an APB error response for accesses with an invalid requester attribute.

### 4.2 Requester Filtering

The module shall support programmable and integration-time requester attributes for access to mailbox, fuse, and TRNG regions.

- Only requesters whose attributes are marked valid shall be allowed to access these protected regions.
- The valid requester attributes shall be lockable so that they cannot be changed after initialization.
- If a requester attribute is not valid, the access shall be dropped and reported as an error.

### 4.3 Register Interface

The APB interface shall expose the following functional register groups:

- Mailbox control, status, and data registers
- Fuse programming registers
- Security state and lifecycle control
- Watchdog timer registers
- Timer and interrupt control registers
- SHA accelerator registers
- TRNG data and control registers when external TRNG mode is used
- Generic input/output register windows
- Boot control and status registers

## 5. Mailbox Behavior

The module shall implement the Caliptra mailbox protocol for communication between the SoC and the internal processor.

### 5.1 Lock Ownership

The mailbox shall support exclusive ownership.

- When the mailbox is unlocked, an SoC requester that reads the lock register shall receive a value indicating that it has acquired the lock.
- While the mailbox is locked, any other SoC requester that reads the lock register shall receive a value indicating that the mailbox is busy.
- The lock owner shall be identified by its requester attribute.
- There shall be no fairness arbitration; ownership is first come, first served.
- The lock shall be released when the current owner completes the mailbox flow and clears the execute control.

### 5.2 Sending a Command

A SoC requester that owns the lock shall be allowed to:

1. Write the command value.
2. Write the data length.
3. Write data into the mailbox data-in region.
4. Write the execute bit to begin processing.

When the execute bit is set, the module shall generate an interrupt to the internal processor indicating that a command is available.

### 5.3 Receiving a Response

When the internal processor has populated the mailbox with response data, the module shall assert the data-available output to the SoC. The SoC may then read the command, data length, and data-out region.

When the mailbox flow is complete, the module shall assert the flow-done output.

### 5.4 Protocol Violations

The module shall detect mailbox protocol violations, including:

- Writes to mailbox registers without first acquiring the lock.
- Writes or reads by an SoC requester that is not the current lock owner.
- Out-of-order register accesses by the current lock owner.

On a protocol violation, the module shall:

- Record the error in a non-fatal error register.
- Assert the non-fatal error output.
- Generate an interrupt to the internal processor.
- Enter an error state for out-of-order violations.

In the mailbox error state, the lock shall be preserved, and normal operation shall be restored only by a system reset or by an internal force-unlock write from firmware.

## 6. Security State, Debug, and Scan

### 6.1 Security State Capture

The module shall latch the security state input when Caliptra is released from reset. Until the security state is validly captured, the module shall default to the most secure state:

- Production lifecycle
- Debug locked

The latched security state shall be used for all security decisions during the current power session.

### 6.2 Debug Mode

When the security state indicates that debug mode is allowed, the module shall:

- Enable JTAG debug access to the processor and subsystem.
- Use deterministic debug constants in place of the real obfuscation key, UDS seed, and field entropy.
- Present debug values to cryptographic engines that consume these secrets.

When a transition from locked to unlocked debug state is detected, the module shall:

- Clear all device secrets.
- Clear key vault entries.
- Clear de-obfuscation state.
- Clear internal cryptographic state that may contain secret-derived values.
- Notify firmware through an interrupt.

### 6.3 Scan Mode

The module shall accept a scan-mode input. Scan mode shall be treated as an insecure state.

- When scan mode is asserted, the module shall use debug constant values for secrets.
- On a low-to-high transition of scan mode, the module shall clear all secrets and key material.
- The module shall not allow secret values to be scanned out.

### 6.4 Fatal Error Secret Clearing

If a fatal error is indicated, the module shall clear all secrets and key material using the same secret-clearing behavior required for debug or scan entry.

### 6.5 Secret Clearing

Secret clearing shall include at least:

- The latched obfuscation key.
- Obfuscated UDS and field entropy.
- Key vault entries.
- Data vault contents.
- De-obfuscation engine state.
- Any in-progress cryptographic state that uses secret material.

The module shall complete secret clearing without requiring firmware assistance, and shall also notify firmware so that firmware can perform any additional required cleanup.

### 6.6 JTAG Test-Data Output Enable

The module shall expose the JTAG test-data output-enable as a top-level output to the SoC. The output-enable shall indicate when the internal debug TAP is driving the serial test-data output, so that an external test-data driver is enabled only while scan data is being shifted out and remains disabled otherwise.

## 7. Clock and Reset Domains

The module shall support asynchronous reset assertion and synchronous reset deassertion for external reset inputs.

The JTAG interface shall be treated as a separate clock domain. JTAG accesses shall be synchronized into the main module clock domain when necessary to prevent metastability.

The module shall support the option to force the internal processor into reset permanently for integration bring-up or debug configurations. In that configuration, the processor shall not execute code after reset.

## 8. Interrupt and Error Reporting

### 8.1 SoC Error Outputs

The module shall provide two error indication outputs to the SoC:

- A fatal error output, asserted for unrecoverable hardware, security, or watchdog failures.
- A non-fatal error output, asserted for recoverable errors, such as mailbox protocol violations or certain cryptographic errors.

Error conditions shall be recorded in status registers that the SoC can read and clear as appropriate.

### 8.2 Processor Interrupts

The module shall aggregate interrupts from all internal sources and deliver them to the processor as a single external interrupt vector.

Interrupt sources shall include:

- Error and notification events from each cryptographic engine.
- Error and notification events from the SoC interface.
- Mailbox command-ready notifications.
- Timer interrupts.
- Watchdog timeout interrupts.

Vector assignment shall follow the device specification, with vector 0 reserved and the first external source mapped to vector 1.

### 8.3 Non-Maskable Interrupt

The module shall provide a non-maskable interrupt to the processor. The NMI vector shall be programmable by firmware.

NMI shall be asserted on fatal watchdog timeout or other catastrophic events requiring immediate firmware attention.

### 8.4 Timer Interrupts

The module shall provide programmable timer registers that generate a processor interrupt when the current time reaches a programmed compare value. The timer frequency and compare values shall be configurable.

## 9. Watchdog Timer

The module shall implement a two-stage watchdog timer.

Behavior:

- Timer 1 and Timer 2 shall each have independent enable, restart, and 64-bit timeout value controls.
- In the default cascade mode, only Timer 1 counts. When Timer 1 times out, it shall issue an error interrupt to the processor and start Timer 2.
- If Timer 2 times out in cascade mode, the module shall assert a fatal error output and an NMI to the processor.
- If Timer 2 is enabled independently, both timers shall count independently, and Timer 2 timeout shall generate an error interrupt rather than a fatal error.
- Restarting the timers shall reset the count values.
- Disabling and re-enabling the timers shall not automatically restart them from zero unless the restart control is also set.

## 10. Internal Processor and Memory Map

The module shall integrate a 32-bit RISC-V processor core with:

- A 32-bit AHB-Lite instruction-fetch interface.
- A 32-bit AHB-Lite load/store interface.
- Debug interface support.
- Direct memory access slave interface support.
- 31 external interrupt inputs.
- Reset vector at address 0.
- Programmable NMI vector.

The module shall provide the following address regions to the processor:

- Boot ROM: 48 KiB at base address `0x0000_0000`
- Cryptographic subsystem: 512 KiB at base address `0x1000_0000`
- Peripherals: 32 KiB at base address `0x2000_0000`
- SoC interface: 256 KiB at base address `0x3000_0000`
- Instruction closely-coupled memory: 128 KiB at base address `0x4000_0000`
- Data closely-coupled memory: 128 KiB at base address `0x5000_0000`
- Processor interrupt controller: 256 MiB at base address `0x6000_0000`

The internal AHB data path shall be 64 bits wide, but slave devices shall be natively 32 bits. Therefore, the module shall support 32-bit and smaller transfers only; 64-bit transfers are not supported and may not produce valid results.

### 10.1 Instruction Memory Write Lock

The module shall provide a write-lock mechanism for instruction memory accesses performed through the DMA path.

- When the lock is active, DMA writes to the instruction memory region shall be blocked.
- Blocked write attempts shall be reported to firmware.
- The lock shall be released during the firmware-update reset flow.

## 11. Memory Interfaces

### 11.1 Mailbox SRAM

The module shall provide an SRAM interface for the mailbox data buffer.

The interface shall include:

- Chip select.
- Write enable.
- Address.
- Write data.
- Read data.

The data path shall include both data and ECC bits. The module shall preserve the ECC field as an opaque value; the ECC is generated and checked by the mailbox SRAM controller.

### 11.2 Instruction ROM

The module shall provide a read-only memory interface for the boot ROM.

The interface shall include:

- Chip select.
- Address.
- Read data.

The module shall never issue writes on this interface. Writes to the boot ROM address region shall have no effect.

### 11.3 Processor Local Memory Export

The module shall export the tightly coupled instruction and data memory interfaces so that the physical SRAMs can be implemented outside the module.

The exported interface shall include per-bank:

- Clock enable.
- Write enable.
- Address.
- Write data.
- Read data.
- ECC bits.

The external memory implementation shall provide the storage and read data back to the processor. The module shall support the configured memory size, bank count, and ECC width.

## 12. Cryptographic Services

The module shall provide the following cryptographic capabilities to internal firmware through memory-mapped registers:

- SHA-512, SHA-384, SHA-512/224, and SHA-512/256 hashing.
- SHA-256 and SHA-224 hashing.
- HMAC-SHA-384.
- Deterministic ECDSA P-384 key generation, signing, and verification.
- De-obfuscation of UDS and field entropy using the obfuscation key.
- LMS/Winternitz chain acceleration through the SHA-256 engine.

The module shall provide status and interrupt indications for completion of cryptographic operations. Secret key material used by these operations shall be held in dedicated key vault storage and shall not be readable by firmware.

### 12.1 Key Vault

The module shall provide a key vault with multiple 512-bit key slots.

- Key slots shall not be directly readable or writable by firmware.
- Firmware shall control key slots through control/status registers.
- Key slots shall be lockable to prevent modification or use.
- Key slots shall be cleared on reset or when a clear command is issued.
- Key vault entries shall be cleared on debug/scan entry and fatal error.

### 12.2 PCR Vault

The module shall provide a platform configuration register vault with multiple 384-bit entries.

- PCR entries shall be readable by firmware.
- PCR entries shall support clear and hash-extend operations.
- PCR entries shall be locked against clearing when their lock bit is set.
- The module shall support a PCR signing flow that hashes all PCRs with a nonce and signs the digest using a designated key vault slot.

### 12.3 Data Vault

The module shall provide a set of generic scratch registers that can be locked and cleared on either cold reset or warm reset. Data vault contents shall be usable by firmware as temporary secure storage.

## 13. Optional Peripherals

### 13.1 QSPI

When the optional QSPI controller is enabled, the module shall provide a QSPI master interface supporting:

- Two chip-select outputs.
- Standard SPI, Dual SPI, and Quad SPI transfers.
- Programmable SPI clock polarity and phase.
- Programmable clock divider.
- TX and RX FIFOs.
- Configurable command segments, including transmit, receive, and dummy cycles.

When the optional QSPI controller is not enabled, the QSPI outputs shall be driven to their inactive low state.

### 13.2 UART

When the optional UART controller is enabled, the module shall provide a serial UART interface with:

- Programmable baud rate.
- Transmit and receive data paths.
- FIFO status and interrupt outputs.
- Support for standard serial frames with start, data, and stop bits.

When the optional UART controller is not enabled, no UART interface shall be present.

### 13.3 Integrated TRNG

When the integrated TRNG is enabled, the module shall include:

- An entropy source that accepts a physical noise-source input.
- A CSRNG block that generates random data for firmware.
- A request output that tells the SoC to enable or provide entropy.
- A valid/data input pair used to sample entropy from the physical source.

The module shall support firmware commands to instantiate, reseed, generate, update, and uninstantiate the CSRNG. Generated random data shall be read through the CSRNG register interface.

The physical noise source shall be sampled only when valid is asserted. The request output shall remain asserted while entropy is required.

### 13.4 External TRNG API

When the integrated TRNG is not enabled, the module shall provide an external TRNG hardware request interface.

The module shall:

- Assert the TRNG request output when Caliptra firmware or internal hardware needs entropy.
- Wait for the SoC to write random data into the architectural TRNG data registers.
- Wait for the SoC to indicate that the data is valid.
- Deassert the TRNG request once valid entropy has been received.

The external TRNG data path shall be protected by requester filtering. If the TRNG requester lock is not programmed, the module shall not accept TRNG data from any SoC entity.

## 14. Generic I/O

The module shall provide a 64-bit generic input bus and a 64-bit generic output bus.

- The generic input bus values shall be readable by firmware through registers.
- Any change on any bit of the generic input bus shall generate a notification interrupt to the processor.
- The generic output bus shall be driven from firmware-programmable output registers.

## 15. Configuration-Dependent Behavior

The module shall be build-time configurable in the following ways:

- Inclusion or exclusion of the integrated TRNG.
- Inclusion or exclusion of the internal UART.
- Inclusion or exclusion of the internal QSPI.
- Ability to force the processor into reset.
- Integration-time requester attribute overrides.
- Integration-time default mailbox requester attribute.
- Integration-time fuse requester attribute override.

The module shall maintain the same security, reset, boot, mailbox, and error-reporting behavior regardless of which optional peripherals are included.

# Behavioral Design Specification: VeeR EL2 Integration Wrapper

## 1. Overview

This module is the top-level integration wrapper for a 32-bit VeeR EL2 RISC-V processor core and its tightly-coupled memory subsystem. It provides the external interfaces needed by the rest of the system for processor execution, instruction fetch, data access, debug, interrupt handling, trace, memory export, and test control.

The wrapper is configured at build time to expose either an AXI4 or an AHB-Lite bus fabric. The non-selected bus protocol is not present or is tied to benign inactive values.

## 2. Clocks and Resets

- The wrapper is synchronous to a single core clock input.
- Two active-low reset inputs are provided:
  - a main functional reset that initializes the processor and core memory logic.
  - a debug reset that initializes the JTAG/debug access logic.
- Reset assertion is asynchronous. Deassertion must be synchronized to the clock by the source.
- While the main reset is active, the processor shall not execute instructions and no functional memory or bus transactions shall be generated.
- The debug reset may be asserted independently of the main reset. The debug access path must not cause functional transactions when the main reset is active.
- The processor shall begin fetching from the word-aligned reset vector provided at the reset-vector input after the main reset is deasserted.

## 3. Processor and Interrupt Behavior

- The wrapped processor is a 32-bit RISC-V core with a 4-stage, scalar, in-order pipeline.
- The processor supports the standard RISC-V integer, compressed, multiply/divide, and selected bit-manipulation extensions.
- The wrapper accepts interrupt requests of the following types:
  - a non-maskable interrupt request with a word-aligned trap vector.
  - a timer interrupt request.
  - a software interrupt request.
  - a vector of external interrupt requests.
- The external interrupt vector is 1-based: bit 1 corresponds to external interrupt vector 1, bit 2 to vector 2, and so on. Vector 0 is not present.
- When the non-maskable interrupt request is asserted, the processor shall take the NMI trap and jump to the supplied NMI vector.
- Timer, software, and external interrupts shall be taken according to the RISC-V privilege specification and the core’s programmable interrupt enable and priority state.
- The wrapper accepts a word-aligned core identifier. This identifier is used by the debug logic to identify the core in multi-core JTAG/debug configurations.

## 4. Instruction Trace Output

- The wrapper shall provide an instruction trace interface for external debug and trace tools.
- The trace interface shall present:
  - the instruction word.
  - the instruction address.
  - an instruction-valid indication.
  - an exception-valid indication.
  - an exception cause.
  - an interrupt-valid indication.
  - the trap value associated with an exception or interrupt.
- For every retired instruction, the instruction-valid indication shall be asserted and the instruction word and address shall be presented.
- If the retired instruction took an exception or interrupt, the corresponding qualifier, cause, and trap value shall be presented alongside the trace information.

## 5. Bus Interfaces

Only the bus protocol selected at build time is active. The wrapper shall behave as described for that protocol.

### 5.1 AXI4 Configuration

When configured for AXI4, the wrapper shall provide:

- Three AXI4 master interfaces:
  - an instruction fetch master interface for instruction reads.
  - a load/store unit master interface for data reads and writes.
  - a debug/system-bus master interface for debug access to the memory-mapped system.
- One AXI4 slave interface for DMA access.

Each AXI4 master interface shall implement the full AXI4 read and write channel handshakes, including address, data, response, and burst control. The wrapper shall generate valid bursts, sizes, IDs, and attributes and shall comply with the AXI4 protocol.

The DMA slave interface shall accept external DMA read and write transactions and deliver them into the processor/memory address map. The wrapper shall generate valid AXI4 responses for the DMA master.

### 5.2 AHB-Lite Configuration

When configured for AHB-Lite, the wrapper shall provide:

- Three AHB-Lite master interfaces:
  - an instruction fetch master interface.
  - a load/store unit master interface.
  - a debug/system-bus master interface.
- One AHB-Lite slave interface for DMA access.

The AHB-Lite master interfaces shall perform 32-bit addressed, 64-bit data transfers and shall drive appropriate transfer type, burst, size, protection, lock, write, data, and response handshakes.

The DMA slave interface shall accept AHB-Lite accesses from an external DMA master and respond according to the AHB-Lite protocol.

### 5.3 Bus Clock Enables

- Each bus interface has an associated clock-enable input to support a clock ratio between the core clock and the bus clock.
- The wrapper shall only advance a bus transaction while the relevant clock enable is asserted.
- If the clock enable is deasserted mid-transaction, the wrapper shall preserve the transaction state and resume the transaction when the enable is asserted again.
- This requirement applies to both master and slave bus interfaces.

## 6. Memory Export

### 6.1 Tightly-Coupled Memory Interface

- The wrapper shall export the processor’s instruction closely-coupled memory (ICCM) and data closely-coupled memory (DCCM) to an external SRAM implementation.
- The exported memory interface is banked and includes, for each bank:
  - a clock enable.
  - a write enable.
  - an address bus.
  - a write-data bus.
  - a read-data bus.
- The number of banks, address widths, and data widths are determined by the core configuration.
- A write shall occur when the clock enable and write enable are active; the write-data value shall be stored at the supplied address.
- A read shall occur when the clock enable is active and the write enable is inactive. The external memory shall return read data after the read address is presented.
- The wrapper is responsible for generating the read/write controls expected by a one-cycle-read external SRAM.

### 6.2 ECC Status

- The wrapper shall provide ECC status outputs for the instruction memory and the data memory.
- For each memory type, the wrapper shall report:
  - a single-bit error status.
  - a double-bit error status.
- The single-bit error status shall be asserted when a single-bit ECC error is detected.
- The double-bit error status shall be asserted when a double-bit or otherwise uncorrectable ECC error is detected.
- These outputs are intended for external reliability and machine-check logic.

## 7. Debug Access

### 7.1 JTAG / DMI Access

- The wrapper shall provide a JTAG debug endpoint with:
  - test clock input.
  - test mode-select input.
  - serial test-data input.
  - serial test-data output.
  - an output-enable for the test-data driver.
  - a JTAG reset input.
- JTAG access shall be translated into DMI read/write transactions.
- A DMI transaction consists of an access-enable, write-enable, address, write data, and read data.
- The DMI address space is split into two regions:
  - a low region for core debug registers.
  - a high region for uncore SoC-interface registers.
- The wrapper shall route each DMI access to either the core side or the uncore side based on the address region.
- The wrapper shall select the read-data source based on the same address-region decode.
- A raw DMI-access indication shall be provided for external debug/clocking logic. It indicates that a DMI access is occurring before final security and address qualification.

### 7.2 Security Qualification

- DMI accesses shall be permitted only when the security state allows debug access.
- Access is permitted when:
  - the security state is not debug-locked, or
  - the security state is debug-locked and the device lifecycle is manufacturing.
- In all other security states, the wrapper shall block both core and uncore register accesses by deasserting the qualified access enables and write enables.
- A blocked access shall have no effect on core or uncore registers.
- The address and write-data values may still be presented, but the qualified enables shall remain inactive.

### 7.3 External Halt/Run Control

- The wrapper shall support external halt/run handshake interfaces for power-management and CPU debug control.
- Each interface accepts asynchronous halt-request and run-request inputs and returns acknowledge outputs.
- A halt request shall cause the processor to halt at an instruction boundary and enter the halted state.
- When the processor is halted, the wrapper shall assert halt acknowledge and halt status.
- A run request shall cause the processor to exit the halted state, resume execution, and assert run acknowledge.
- A debug-mode status shall be asserted whenever the processor is in debug mode. External controllers should not issue halt or run requests while debug mode is active.
- A breakpoint status shall indicate when the processor is halted at a debug breakpoint.
- The reset-run input shall determine the state of the processor after reset:
  - If reset-run is asserted, the processor shall begin executing after reset deassertion.
  - If reset-run is deasserted, the processor shall remain halted until a run request is received.

## 8. Performance and Status Outputs

- The wrapper shall provide four performance-counter event outputs.
- Each output shall toggle whenever the corresponding internal performance counter is incremented.
- These outputs allow external logic to observe selected core event counts without accessing performance-monitor registers.

## 9. Test Mode Inputs

- A scan-mode input shall be supported. When asserted, the wrapper and its embedded processor/memory logic shall operate in scan-test configuration. Functional execution is not guaranteed during scan mode.
- A memory-BIST mode input shall be supported. When asserted, the exported memory interface shall be controlled for memory self-test operation. Normal processor access to memories is not guaranteed while this mode is active.
